title: Muonio takes over wilderness huts from Metsähallitus
seoTitle: Muonio takes over Metsähallitus huts in January
description: Parks & Wildlife Finland and the municipality of Muonio agreed that several wilderness huts and lean-tos move to the municipality at the start of 2027.
dek: The huts at Vuontisjärvi, Kuusikonmaa, Tammikämppä, Pahtavaara and Juuvanrova stay open and free of charge, but from January it is the municipality that maintains them, and it may also rent them out.
heroAlt: Skiers standing beside a low log hut whose roof carries a thick layer of snow, in a spruce forest with a wooded fell slope behind and a clear blue sky above.
heroCaption: The old Mustavaara hut in Muonio in March 2013. The huts that now change hands are elsewhere in Muonio, from Vuontisjärvi to Juuvanrova.

body.text: Parks & Wildlife Finland and the municipality of Muonio have agreed that several hiking structures in the Muonio area move into municipal ownership and maintenance on 1 January 2027. The two announced the arrangement on 26 November 2026. Muonio buys the wilderness huts at Vuontisjärvi, Kuusikonmaa and Tammikämppä, the kota at Vuontisjärvi, the Siepinvaara lean-to and the Tunturijärvi lean-to at Olos, together with the structures of their rest areas, including campfire sites, toilets and woodsheds. The structures are sold in the condition they are in at the time of sale, and a separate land use agreement with Metsähallitus allows them to stay where they stand.

Two further sites pass to the municipality under a use right agreement rather than a sale. At Pahtavaara the package is the wilderness hut, the firewood shelter, the dry toilet and the campfire site. At Juuvanrova it is the hut, the dry toilet, the woodshed, the campfire site and a maintenance store.

For a walker arriving at the door, nothing changes on the ground. The structures that change hands remain in general hiking use, Parks & Wildlife Finland says. This change secures destinations that are important from a local point of view, and when the municipality of Muonio takes on the hiking services they stay in public use, says Jarmo Asell of Parks & Wildlife Finland. He adds that the sites offer alternative destinations and so help even out the visitor pressure on Pallas-Yllästunturi, the most popular national park in Finland.

Nature and the varied hiking routes are central strengths in the area, so moving the structures into municipal ownership was the only right solution, says Laura Enbuska-Mäki, municipal manager of Muonio. In her words the arrangement secures the continuity of local services and creates the conditions for developing them over the long term.
The huts stay open, the maintainer changes

One thing does change for visitors. The municipality may rent out the hiking structures it buys, and it asks anyone interested to contact it. Companies that work with Metsähallitus and use these structures have to make a use right agreement with the municipality of Muonio instead. Hikers will still find the sites on the Luontoon.fi service, into which Muonio will feed the details of the transferred structures through the Lipas database.
Why Metsähallitus is handing sites over

Parks & Wildlife Finland runs hiking services at about 250 destinations of different sizes, with 2 400 complexes of hiking structures, 34 000 individual structures and 13 000 kilometres of routes. Its funding has shrunk considerably, so it has gone through the routes and rest areas of the whole country to direct the money it has at the destinations judged most important, and it has looked for municipalities and other partners for the sites it gives up. Negotiations are under way with other municipalities as well. Metsähallitus says it will go on providing hiking services in all 41 national parks and in the six state hiking areas. The land stays in state ownership in every case, and giving up the upkeep of services does not prevent independent hiking.

items: Vuontisjärvi: the hut stands on the north-west shore of the lake along the Muonio to Hetta snowmobile route, has sleeping places for 4, and Metsähallitus rates it a demanding wilderness destination.
Kuusikonmaa: between the fells of Nivunkitunturi and Särkitunturi, sleeping places for 5, and Metsähallitus warns that there may not be room to sleep.
Tammikämppä: north of lake Luusunjärvi, sleeping places for 4.

Pahtavaara: south of Tupakkalaki on the shore of a small pond, 7 kilometres along a path from the Muotkavaara to Äkäslompolo road in the direction of Olos, sleeping places for 6. The cabin was moved here from Ruostevaara, 2 kilometres away, in 2006.
Juuvanrova: on the top of the Juuvanrova hill, sleeping places for 4.
All of them are modest huts that are open all year round and free to use.

body.text: An open wilderness hut is a shared, unlocked place to rest or spend a night, you cannot book it in advance, and a stay of one or two nights is the limit. Carry a tent or a plan for the night in case the hut is already full when you get there.
A free hut along the way shapes how far you can plan a winter day, and the same is true of other trails in Lapland.
